content:
We often discuss {f : R ->+* S} (hf : Function.Injective). I was thinking, inspired by l[i]'hi style syntax, what if we could say

{f : R ↪+*(hf) S}

to mean {f : R →+* S} (hf : Function.Injective f). Or, {f : R ↪(hf)→+* S} (can bikeshed on syntax). By my loogle-style counting, there would be ~465 declarations that could use this.

Now, unlike l[i]'hi, which is shorthand for providing a proof obligation in a drive-by way, this requires different elaboration of binders in a decl. We do some binder manipulation in the expand_binders% macro, but that is manipulation of one binder into one binder, while I am suggesting one binder into 2.

This is also kinda like variable_alias, but that provides an action to expand variable sections.

However, seems like we'd need special decl elaborators, so we couldn't just use regular theorem or example or variable...?

How might this compare to bundling the injectivity hypothesis into a new type R ↪+* S, with appropriate coercions? (I'm guessing this might have been discussed before, but think it might be useful to mention briefly here again if so :) )

(I will mention re: the suggestion of changing binder elaboration that we unfortunately have very little meta control over binders without overriding all of the declaration commands (as you identify), which is not really a good thing to do :/ So I don't think there is a good way to expand one binder into two at present, unfortunately.)

Yes, we already bundle in some instances, like Embedding. But to me, the category the hom is in seems more natural than defining a type or subtype of it. Because, for example, lets say I have a field hom f : K ->+* L, then the injectivity assumption could be resolved automatically, instead of having to say f.toInjectiveRingHom (by obviously). Additionally, I think it is more natural for many theorems to state their arguments/assumptions for such homs as unbundled.

This came from thinking about how to make Lean easier to read and how a diagram chase/setup would look like in a dream world.
